## 5.7 Handling multiple-hole queries

**In this section we discuss how to drop the simplifying assumption that the query set** $A \subseteq \partial P$ **lies** entirely on a single hole of $P$

**Before we continue, let us remark that in Section 5 we did not fully leverage the fact that the holes’ bounding cycles of a piece of an r-division with few holes contain vertices from** $\partial P$ **exclusively. Indeed, we only used that (i) A lies on a single face h of** $P ,$ **and (ii) that there was no need to report or aggregate vertices lying on the bounding cycle of h – indeed, in a piece of an r-division** with few holes no vertex of $V ( P ) \setminus \partial P$ lies on the bounding cycle of $h .$

In the following, we will slightly relax the problem: define $\hat { O } ^ { * } P$ **to contain all the vertices of** $P$ **on** the bounding cycles of $h _ { 1 } , \ldots , h _ { k }$ , and let $\partial P$ be an arbitrary fixed subset of $\partial ^ { * } P$ **of size** $O ( { \sqrt { r } } )$ **(**but the set $\partial ^ { * } P$ **can be possibly larger). Given** $A \subseteq \partial P$ **, the query’s objective is to aggregate/report** vertices of $\Pi _ { P } ( A ) \setminus \partial ^ { * } P$ **. By the above discussion, the data structure of Section 5 can actually solve this slightly more general problem within the same bounds. Moreover, as discussed in Section 5.2, we no longer use the assumption of Theorem 4.3 that** $\Pi _ { P } ( A ) \cap \partial P = A$ **which was only required to reduce to the acyclic case.**

Denote by $\hat { O } _ { i } ^ { * } P ,$ for $i   =   1 , \ldots , k$ , the vertices of $\hat { O } ^ { * } P$ that lie on the hole $h _ { i }$ **. Recall that** $k = O ( 1 )$ . The sets $\partial _ { 1 } ^ { * } P , \ldots , \partial _ { k } ^ { * } P$ **are not necessarily disjoint. We now describe how to reduce the** problem, roughly speaking, to the case when P has one hole less. The reduction will require $O ( r ^ { 3 } )$ additional preprocessing and will add only $O ( | A | )$ **overhead to the query procedure. The reduction will preserve acyclicity.**

## 5.7.1 Preprocessing

Suppose first that there exist no such $s \in \partial _ { i } ^ { * } P$ and $t \in \partial _ { j } ^ { * } P$ , where $i \neq j$ , that s can reach t in $P .$ This can be clearly checked in $O ( | P | ) = O ( r )$ time by running graph search k times. In this case, we have that $\Pi _ { P } ( A ) \setminus \partial ^ { * } P$ is a disjoint sum of $\Pi _ { P } ( A \cap \partial _ { i } ^ { * } P ) \setminus \partial _ { i } ^ { * } P$ **.** Hence, all we do is simply apply **the preprocessing of Section 5 k times, for each hole** $h _ { i }$ **i**ndependently, i.e., we set $\partial ^ { * } P : = \partial _ { i } ^ { * } P$ **and** $\partial P : = \partial P \cap \partial _ { i } ^ { * } P$ in the i-th single-hole data structure. This takes $\widetilde { O } ( k r ^ { 3 } ) = \widetilde { O } ( r ^ { 3 } )$ **time.**

e eLet us now assume that such s, t exist and pick them so that we can find a simple $s \rightarrow t$ path $Q$ such that $V ( Q ) \cap \partial ^ { * } P = \{ s , t \}$ **(we might possibly have** $s = t )$ **. For example, such a path** $Q$ **can be** found in $O ( r )$ **O(r) time by computing, for each pair of holes of** $P ,$ **a shortest path between these two** holes, and taking the shortest out of these paths as $Q .$ Wlog. let us renumber the sets $\partial _ { i } ^ { * } P$ **so that** $s \in \partial _ { 1 } ^ { * } P$ and $t \in \partial _ { 2 } ^ { * } P$

**For every** $b \in \partial P$ **,** we compute (i) the first vertex firstb on the path $Q$ that b can reach in $P ,$ and (ii) the last vertex las $\mathrm { t } _ { b }$ **on** $Q$ **that can reach b in P. All the vertices** $\mathrm { f i r s t } _ { b }$ **and** $\mathrm { l a s t } _ { b }$ **(that exist) can be computed in** $O ( r )$ **time via graph search (see e.g. [Tho04]).**

Let us obtain a graph $P ^ { \prime }$ from $P$ **by cutting along the path** $Q = u _ { 1 } \ldots u _ { q } = s \to t .$ **. Formally, the** path $Q$ is replaced with two copies $Q ^ { \prime } = u _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } \ldots u _ { q } ^ { \prime }$ and $Q ^ { \prime \prime } = u _ { 1 } ^ { \prime \prime } \ldots u _ { q } ^ { \prime \prime } ,$ , but the copies $u _ { i } ^ { \prime } , u _ { i } ^ { \prime \prime }$ **of the** vertex $u _ { i }$ are not connected. Neither the vertices nor the edges of $Q$ are contained in the graph $P ^ { \prime } ,$ , only $Q ^ { \prime }$ and $Q ^ { \prime \prime }$ are there. For all $v \in V ( P ) \setminus V ( Q )$ **,** for convenience we set $v ^ { \prime } = v ^ { \prime \prime } : = v$ **.** Clearly, $P ^ { \prime }$ is acyclic if $P$ is acyclic.

We set the boundary of $P ^ { \prime }$ **to be:**

$$
\partial P ^ { \prime } : = \partial P \setminus \{ s , t \} \cup \bigcup _ { b \in \partial P } \{ { \operatorname { f i r s t } } _ { b } ^ { \prime } , { \operatorname { f i r s t } } _ { b } ^ { \prime \prime } , { \operatorname { l a s t } } _ { b } ^ { \prime } , { \operatorname { l a s t } } _ { b } ^ { \prime \prime } \} .
$$

Note that the two holes $h _ { 1 } , h _ { 2 }$ of $P$ are merged into a single hole h in $P ^ { \prime }$ **. As a result, and since** all the vertices $\partial P ^ { \prime } \setminus \partial P$ lie on $h ,   P ^ { \prime }$ has less holes (that is, faces containing boundary vertices $\partial P ^ { \prime } )$ than $P .$ Moreover, we have (recall that $\partial ^ { * } P ^ { \prime }$ denotes all vertices on the holes of $P ^ { \prime } )$

$$
\partial ^ { * } P ^ { \prime } : = \partial ^ { * } P \setminus \{ s , t \} \cup V ( Q ^ { \prime } ) \cup V ( Q ^ { \prime \prime } ) .
$$

Observe that $| P ^ { \prime } | \leq 3 | P | = O ( r )$ **a**nd $| \partial P ^ { \prime } | \leq 5 | \partial P |$ so $| \partial P ^ { \prime } | = O ( { \sqrt { r } } )$ **.** We recursively build a data structure supporting desired queries $A ^ { \prime } \subseteq \partial P ^ { \prime }$ on the graph $P ^ { \prime }$ as defined above.

**Finally, for all the subpaths R of** $Q$ **we precompute the aggregate weights of all the vertices of** $V ( R ) \setminus \partial ^ { * } P = V ( R ) \setminus \{ s , t \}$ **.** This can be done in $O ( r ^ { 3 } )$ time using a brute force algorithm.

Since the piece $P$ has initially size $O ( r ) ,   | \partial P |   =   O ( \sqrt { r } )$ and $\partial P$ lies on $k = O ( 1 )$ holes of $P .$ after at most $k - 1$ recursive preprocessing steps we will arrive at the single-hole case (when a pair $s , t$ cannot be found, possibly because $k = 1 )$ . In each of the recursive data structures, the input piece has size $2 ^ { O ( k ) } \cdot O ( r )   =   O ( r )$ **,** and has $\left| \partial P \right|   =   2 ^ { O ( k ) } \cdot O ( \sqrt { r } )   =   O ( \sqrt { r } )$ . At each of the $O ( 1 )$ **r**ecursive levels, the additional preprocessing take**s** $O ( r ^ { 3 } )$ **t**ime.

## 5.7.2 Query

**Given** $A   \subseteq   \partial P$ **, the query procedure is as follows. Since there are no paths between boundary vertices on distinct holes, we can aggregate the results in an obvious way. This is justified by the fact that** $\Pi _ { P } ( A ) \setminus \partial ^ { * } P$ is a disjoint union of the $O ( 1 )$ sets $\Pi _ { P } ( A \cap \partial _ { i } ^ { * } P ) \setminus \partial ^ { * } P$ **. Clearly, the query algorithm** runs in $\widetilde { O } ( | A | )$ time in this case.

eOtherwise, if P is not leaf-level in the recursion, let ≺ denote the natural order on vertices of the path Q. Again, we have $f \preceq \operatorname { f i r s t } _ { a } \preceq c \preceq d \preceq \operatorname { l a s t } _ { b } \preceq l$ . Moreover, S is preserved in $P ^ { \prime }$ **a**s wlog. the path $S ^ { \prime \prime }   =   c ^ { \prime \prime }   \rightarrow   d ^ { \prime \prime }$ . But then $Q ^ { \prime \prime } [ f ^ { \prime \prime } , c ^ { \prime \prime } ] \cdot S ^ { \prime \prime } \cdot Q ^ { \prime \prime } [ d ^ { \prime \prime } , l ^ { \prime \prime } ]$ is a $f ^ { \prime \prime } \rightarrow l ^ { \prime \prime }$ path in $P ^ { \prime }$ that goes through v. Since $f ^ { \prime \prime } , l ^ { \prime \prime } \in A ^ { \prime }$ , we again obtain $v \in \Pi _ { P ^ { \prime } } ( A ^ { \prime } ) \setminus \partial ^ { * } P ^ { \prime }$ , as desired. □

When queried about the set A, the recursive data structures are passed a set $A ^ { \prime }$ with $| A ^ { \prime } | =$ $| A | + O ( 1 ) = O ( | A | )$ . As a result, the query time is dominated by the $\widetilde { O } ( | A ^ { \prime } | ) = \widetilde { O } ( | A | )$ **time used** e e**by the bottommost single-hole data structure. This finishes the proof of Theorem 4.3.**

## 5.8 The existential reachability data structure

**In this section, we prove the following.**

**Lemma 5.3. In** $\tilde { O } ( r )$ **t**ime one can construct a data structure maintaining an (initially empty) set $Z \subseteq \partial P \cap V ( h )$ eand supporting the following operations in O(polylog n) time:

• **insert or delete a single** $b \in \partial P \cap V ( h )$ **either to or from Z.**

$f o r$ any query vertex $v \in ( \partial P \cap V ( h ) ) \setminus Z _ { . }$ , find any $z \in Z$ (if exists) that v can reach in $P$

**We will use the following property of reachability between vertices lying on a single face of a planar digraph P essentially proved in [IKŁS17].**

**Lemma 5.12. [IKŁS17] Let the vertices Y lie on a single face h of a planar digraph P. Then in** $\widetilde { O } ( | P | + | Y | ^ { 2 } )$ time one can compute $O ( | Y | )$ pairs of subsets $S _ { i } , T _ { i } \subseteq Y$ **such that:**

1. For any i, the elements $T _ { i }$ have an associated linear order $\preceq _ { i }$ .

2. For any i and $s \in S _ { i }$ , there exist such vertices $l _ { i , s } , r _ { i , s }$ that for any $t \in T _ { i } ,$ **s can reach t in P** $\mathit { i f f } \: l _ { i , s } \preceq _ { i } t \preceq _ { i } r _ { i , s }$

**3. Every** $v \in Y$ **i**s contained in $O ( \log | Y | )$ subsets $S _ { i }$ and $O ( \log | Y | )$ subsets $T _ { i }$ .

4. For any $u , v \in Y$ , if u can reach v in P, then there exists such i that $( u , v ) \in S _ { i } \times T _ { i }$

**Proof sketch. Split Y into two disjoint parts A, B such that** $A \cup B = Y ,   | A | , | B |   \leq   \lceil | Y | / 2 \rceil$ **, and both A, B appear consecutively on h. Let T denote the vertices of B that can be reached from some vertex of A in** $P .$ **Similarly, let S denote the vertices of A that can reach B in P. Let ≺ be the counterclockwise order on** $T$ **starting with the vertex that appears earliest after a vertex of A in the counterclockwise order of** $Y$ **on h. One can easily prove (see [IKŁS17]) that each** $s \in S$ **can in fact reach some number of vertices that appear consecutively in T. As a result, there exist such** $l _ { s } , r _ { s } \in T$ that for any $t \in T$ , s can reach t in P iff $l _ { s } \preceq t \preceq r _ { s }$

**We include the pair** $( S , T )$ **along with the order** $\preceq ,$ **and the vertices** $\{ l _ { s } , r _ { s }   :   s   \in   S \}$ **in the constructed family. The obtained pair encodes the reachability from the vertices A to vertices B in P: if** $a \in A$ **can reach** $b \in B$ **in** $T$ **then clearly** $a \in S ,   b \in T$ **. Note that the subsets** $S , T$ **can be** constructed in $\widetilde { O } ( | Y | ^ { 2 } )$ **time if only we can answer reachability queries in P in** $O ( \operatorname { p o l y l o g } n )$ **time.** eThis is indeed possible after $\widetilde { O } ( | P | )$ time preprocessing [Tho04].

eSymmetrically we can deal with the reachability from the vertices B to the vertices A in P. It remains to handle reachability between pairs of vertices inside the set A, and between pairs inside B. This is done recursively. Since $| A | , | B | \leq \lceil | Y | / 2 \rceil$ , each vertex of the original input set $Y$ will appear in $O ( \log | Y | )$ recursive calls, and thus in $O ( \log | Y | )$ sets $S _ { i }$ or $T _ { i }$ **.** It is easy to check that the algorithm produces all the pairs $( S _ { i } , T _ { i } )$ **i**n $\widetilde { O } ( | \dot { Y } | ^ { 2 } )$ **time.** □

Proof of Lemma 5.3. We first compute the sets $( S _ { i } , T _ { i } )$ from Lemma 5.12 applied to $Y : = \partial P { \cap } V ( h )$ (along with the orderings $\prec _ { i } .$ , and all the vertices $l _ { i , v } , r _ { i , v } )$ **i**n $\widetilde { O } ( | P |   +   | \partial P | ^ { 2 } ) = \widetilde { O } ( r )$ time. The data structure simply stores the sets $T _ { i } \cap Z$ efor all i sorted according to $\preceq _ { i }$ e, each of them in a balanced binary search tree. Note that when an element b is inserted or removed from $Z ,$ **i**t is enough to update $O ( \log r )$ sets $T _ { i } \cap Z$ **a**s b is contained in $O ( \log r )$ sets $T _ { i }$

**To answer a query, that is, find a vertex** $z \in Z$ **reachable from a query vertex** $v ,$ **for each of the** $O ( \log r )$ **indices i such that** $v \in S _ { i }$ **we check whether the set** $T _ { i } \cap Z$ **contains an element z between** $l _ { i , s }$ **and** $r _ { i , s }$ **i**nclusive, wrt. $\preceq _ { i }$ . This clearly takes $O ( \log r )$ **time. By Lemma 5.12, s can reach a vertex in Z if and only if at least one z is found this way.**

We conclude that both the update and the query time of the data structure is $O ( \log ^ { 2 } r )$ □

## 6 Fully dynamic #SSR in planar digraphs

**In this section, we sketch how a data structure summarized by the below lemma can be obtained.**

Lemma 6.1. Let $G$ be a planar digraph subject to planarity-preserving edge insertions and deletions. There exists a data structure with $\widetilde { O } ( n ^ { 4 / 5 } )$ **worst-case update time supporting counting the** vertices reachable from a query vertex s in $\tilde { O } ( n ^ { 4 / \tilde { 5 } } )$ **time.**

**We again use the same template as in Sections 3 and 4: as a base, we maintain an r-division R** with few holes, along with the piecewise reachability certificates $X _ { P }$

In addition, we leverage the additively-weighted Voronoi diagram data structure of $\mathrm { [ G K M ^ { + } 2 1 ] }$ Before stating the interface and characteristics of that data structure, we need to introduce some more notation. Suppose H is a non-negatively weighted plane digraph. Let $\partial H \subseteq V ( H )$ be the set of vertices of H lying on some $O ( 1 )$ fixed faces of H (and containing all vertices of these faces) and such that every $v \in V ( H )$ is reachable from ∂H in H. Let $\omega : \partial H \rightarrow$ R be a weight function such that for any $v \in V ( H ) ,   \omega ( s ) + \mathrm { d i s t } _ { H } ( s , v )$ has a unique minimizer $s \in \partial H$ **.** The additively weighted Voronoi diagram wrt. ω is the partition of $V ( H )$ into disjoint subsets (cells) $\operatorname { V o r } ( s ) ,   s \in \partial H$ , such that $\operatorname { V o r } ( s )$ contains precisely the vertices v such that s minimizes $\omega ( s ) + \mathrm { d i s t } _ { H } ( s , v )$ . Note that by our assumptions on H, if $v \in \operatorname { V o r } ( s )$ , then $\omega ( s ) + \mathrm { d i s t } _ { H } ( s , v ) \neq \infty$ . The complexity $| \partial \mathrm { V o r } ( s ) |$ of $\operatorname { V o r } ( s )$ is defined to be the number of faces of H whose vertices include elements **of** $\operatorname { V o r } ( s )$ **and** at least two other cells. One can prove that $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { s \in \partial H } | \partial \mathrm { V o r } ( s ) | = O ( | \partial H | ) [ \mathrm { G K M ^ { + } 2 1 } ] } \end{array}$

Theorem 6.2. $\mathrm { [ G K M ^ { + } 2 1 ] }$ Let H be as defined above. In $\widetilde { O } \left( | H | \cdot | \partial H | ^ { 2 } \right)$ **one can construct a data** e**structure such that for any ω satisfying the assumptions outlined above, it can build a representation of the additively-weighted Voronoi diagram wrt.** $\omega$ **in** $\widetilde { O } ( | \partial H | )$ **time. The representation allows,** among others, computing all the cell sizes $| \mathrm { V o r } ( s ) | ,   s \in \partial H$ , in $\widetilde { O } ( | \partial H | )$ total time.

**Proof sketch. This is essentially a special case of** $\mathrm { [ G K M ^ { + } 2 1 }$ **, Theorem 1.1]. There, it is stated that** after the representation is built, one can compute, for any $s \in \partial H$ , the furthest vertex $v \in \operatorname { V o r } ( s )$ $( \mathrm { i . e . } ,   v$ **maximizing** $\omega ( s )$ **+dist** $\iota _ { H } ( s , v ) )$ **in** $\widetilde { O } ( | \partial \mathrm { V o r } ( s ) | )$ **time. But in** $\mathrm { [ G K M ^ { + } 2 1 }$ **, Section** $7 ]$ **, where this** e**functionality is described, it is evident that within the same time bound one can in fact aggregate over** $\operatorname { V o r } ( s )$ **(that is, compute the maximum or** $\mathbf { e . g . }$ **, sum) arbitrary vertex labels** $\ell ( v )$ **(which could** even dependent on $^ { s ; }$ as long as they are computable in $\widetilde { O } ( | H | \cdot | \partial H | ^ { 2 } )$ **total additional time). Therefore, if we assign the label 1 to every vertex of** $H$ **e**, in $\widetilde { O } ( | \partial \mathrm { V o r } ( s ) | )$ time one can compute $| \mathrm { V o r } ( s ) |$ . Through all $s \in | \partial H |$ , this is $\widetilde { O } ( | \partial H | )$ e time as mentioned before. □

**For each piece** $P ,$ **besides the certificate** $X _ { P }$ **, we additionally maintain a data structure** $\mathcal { A } \mathcal { V } _ { P }$ **of** Theorem 6.2 for a $`` proxy''   P'  ''$ **obtained from** $P$ **by removing all the vertices** $v \in V ( P )$ **unreachable** from $\partial P ,$ . Observe that $\mathcal { A } \mathcal { V } _ { P }$ can be computed in $\widetilde { O } ( | P | \cdot ( | \widetilde { \partial } P | ) ^ { 2 } ) = \widetilde { O } ( r ^ { 2 } )$ **time. By Theorem 2.1,** e eupdating R along with all other associated piecewise data structures costs $\widetilde { O } ( r ^ { 2 } )$ **worst-case time.**

**Upon query about the number of vertices reachable from** $s   \in   V$ **e**, we proceed as follows. We **first compute the subset** $S \subseteq \partial { \mathcal { R } }$ **of boundary vertices reachable from s in G by running graph** search from s on the graph $P _ { s } \cup X = P _ { s } \cup \textstyle \bigcup _ { P \in \mathcal { R } } X _ { P }$ **, where** $P _ { s }$ **is an arbitrarily chosen piece with** containing s. This is correct by Lemma 3.3 and costs $\widetilde { O } ( r   +   n / \sqrt { r } )$ **time. From the graph search we** also retrieve the vertices $T \subseteq V ( P _ { s } ) \setminus \partial P _ { s }$ ethat s can reach. Then, for each $P \neq P _ { s }$ **we construct a** weight function $\omega _ { P }$ such that if $\partial P   \cap   S = \{ a _ { 1 } , \ldots , a _ { k } \}$ and $\partial P \backslash S = \{ b _ { 1 } , \ldots , b _ { l } \}$ , then: $\omega ( a _ { i } ) : = i   \cdot   M$ for all i and $\omega ( b _ { j } ) : = ( k + j )$ **· M for all** $j ,$ **where** $M = V ( P )$ **. Note that since dist** ${ } _ { P ^ { \prime } } ( \partial P , v ) < M$ **for** any $v \in V ( P ^ { \prime } )$ , the cell is uniquely determined for every $v \in V ( P ^ { \prime } )$ **. Namely, if** $v$ **can be reached** from $a _ { i } \in \partial P \cap S$ in $P ^ { \prime }$ , and $i$ is minimized (and thus s can reach v through $S )$ , then $v \in \operatorname { V o r } ( a _ { i } )$ Otherwise, v can be reached from some $b _ { j } \in \partial P \setminus S$ **in** $P ,$ **where** $j$ **is minimized (and s cannot reach** v through S), and then $v \in \mathrm { V o r } ( b _ { j } )$ . We conclude that $\textstyle \bigcup _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } \operatorname { V o r } ( a _ { i } )$ **contains precisely the vertices** $S _ { P } \subseteq V ( P )$ **(including** $\partial P \cap S )$ **that s can reach via paths through** $\partial P$ **. By Theorem 6.2, their** number $\begin{array} { r } { | S _ { P } | = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } | \mathrm { V o r } ( a _ { i } ) | } \end{array}$ can be computed in $\tilde { O } ( \sqrt { r } )$ **time. In fact, these are all vertices that s can reach in** $P ;$ **since** $P \neq P _ { s }$ **, either** $s \notin V ( P )$ **or** $s \in \partial \mathcal { R }$ **, so every vertex in** $P$ **can be reached from s only via some boundary vertex of** $P$ **anyway. We conclude that we can count vertices reachable from s in G by computing:**

$$
| S | + | T | + \sum _ { P _ { s } \neq P \in \mathcal { R } } \left( | S _ { P } | - | S \cap \partial P | \right) .
$$

The query time is thus $\widetilde { O } ( r + n / \sqrt { r } )$ . By picking $r = n ^ { 2 / 5 }$ **, we make both the query time and the** worst-case update time $\widetilde { O } ( n ^ { 4 / 5 } )$
